commands.tooltip: Installs firebase-tools, the official Firebase command-line tool, as a global npm package so the firebase command works anywhere. Requires Node.js and npm. Run firebase --version afterward to confirm the install, then firebase login to authenticate.

commands.desc: Install the Firebase CLI via install script
commands.tooltip: Downloads and runs Firebase's official install script, which detects your operating system and sets up the firebase command without needing Node.js or npm. Piping a remote script into bash always carries risk, so review the script at firebase.tools first. On macOS, curl -sL https://firebase.tools | upgrade=true bash updates an existing install.

Prints the installed firebase-tools version number, which is handy for bug reports and for checking whether you are on a recent release. Firebase CLI v13 and later are the current generation; older major versions drop deprecated commands. Update with npm install -g firebase-tools@latest.

commands.desc: Log in to Firebase with a Google account
commands.tooltip: Opens a browser to authenticate the CLI with your Google account and grants access to your Firebase projects. Your credentials are cached locally, so later commands run without re-authenticating. Run firebase projects:list afterward to confirm the login worked. Use firebase login --reauth to force a fresh sign-in.

Starts the browser sign-in flow again even though the CLI already has cached credentials. Use it when switching Google accounts, after a password change, or when commands start failing with authorization errors. The existing token is replaced once you complete the new login.

commands.desc: Log in without a local callback server
commands.tooltip: Authenticates on machines without a usable localhost, such as remote servers and some CI runners. The CLI prints a URL to open on any device with a browser, then asks you to paste back the authorization code. Use firebase login:ci instead when you need a token for headless automation.

commands.desc: Generate an access token for CI systems
commands.tooltip: Produces a refresh token that lets firebase commands run without interactive login, typically stored as the FIREBASE_TOKEN environment variable in CI pipelines. Run it once on a machine with a browser and treat the printed token like a password — anyone holding it can access your projects. Google now recommends Application Default Credentials over tokens for CI.

Removes the cached Google credentials from your machine, so the next firebase command that needs auth will prompt you to log in again. Useful on shared machines or when you suspect your stored token was compromised. Pass an email address, like firebase logout me@example.com, to sign out a specific account.

commands.desc: List all Firebase projects you can access
commands.tooltip: Prints every Firebase project available to the logged-in account, each with its project ID and display name. Run this right after firebase login as a sanity check. Use the project ID from the list with firebase use or the -P flag to target a specific project.

Creates a Google Cloud project and adds Firebase to it in one step, using my-app as the project ID. Add -n "My App" to set a display name, or -o ORGANIZATION_ID to create it under a Google Cloud organization. The interactive prompts ask for a display name; run it inside a project directory to use the new project immediately.

Makes my-app the active project for the current directory, so commands like firebase deploy target it without extra flags. The choice is recorded in the .firebaserc file and affects only this directory. Run firebase use with no arguments to see the current alias list, or pass -P my-app on any command to override per-invocation.

Prompts you to pick another Firebase project and assign it an alias, then stores the mapping in the .firebaserc file of the current directory. Aliases let you switch between environments, for example staging and prod, with firebase use staging. Commit .firebaserc to share the aliases with your team.

Removes the active project from the current directory, so commands that need a project will error until you run firebase use PROJECT_ID again. Handy when you are about to switch context or when a directory should not implicitly target any project.

commands.desc: Alias a project for quick switching
commands.tooltip: Associates the alias staging with the project my-app in the current directory's .firebaserc file, without the interactive prompts of firebase use --add. Later commands like firebase use staging or firebase deploy -P staging resolve to my-app. Remove an alias later with firebase use --unalias staging.

Deletes the alias staging from the current directory's .firebaserc file, leaving the underlying Firebase project untouched. The alias no longer resolves, so any command that referenced it will fail until you pick a new project. This only edits local configuration, never the Firebase project itself.

commands.desc: Initialize Firebase in the current directory
commands.tooltip: Walks you through choosing a Firebase project and the products to configure, then writes firebase.json and .firebaserc into the directory. It also generates product scaffolding such as functions/index.js and firestore.rules. Re-run it later to add more products, or restrict it with a feature argument like firebase init hosting.

commands.desc: Initialize using a specific Firebase project
commands.tooltip: Skips the project-selection prompt and wires the current directory to the my-app project, which is useful in scripts and CI. You still pick which products to set up interactively. The chosen project becomes the default alias written to .firebaserc.

Sets up Firebase Hosting in the current directory: it asks for a public directory (commonly public) and creates a hosting block in firebase.json plus an index.html starter. The rest of your Firebase products remain untouched. Deploy the result with firebase deploy --only hosting.

Scaffolds the functions/ directory with a package.json and an index.js or index.ts entry point, and asks whether to use TypeScript, ESLint, and npm dependencies. It also registers the functions codebase in firebase.json. Deploy the resulting code with firebase deploy --only functions.

Creates firestore.rules and firestore.indexes.json in the current directory, ready to hold your security rules and composite index definitions. The CLI may also offer to deploy them immediately. Push changes later with firebase deploy --only firestore:rules or firebase deploy --only firestore:indexes.

Adds an emulators block to firebase.json defining ports for each local emulator (for example Firestore on 8080 and Auth on 9099), and can download the emulator binaries. The emulators let you run your backend entirely on your machine without touching production. Start them with firebase emulators:start.

Shows the deploy targets defined for the current project, such as a hosting target grouping several sites under one name. Targets are created with firebase target:apply and let firebase deploy --only target-name push to multiple resources at once.

commands.desc: Map a deploy target to resources
commands.tooltip: Binds the target name my-site to the Hosting site my-site-id for the active project, then writes the mapping to .firebaserc. Afterward, firebase deploy --only hosting:my-site deploys to that site. Run firebase target hosting to verify the mapping.

commands.desc: Open project pages in the browser
commands.tooltip: Launches your browser at the Firebase console pages for the active project, with a menu of destinations such as Hosting, Functions logs, and Database. Pass a link name like firebase open hosting:site to jump straight to a destination non-interactively.

Pushes every deployable resource in your firebase.json to the active project: Hosting content, Cloud Functions, Firestore and Storage rules, Firestore indexes, and more. It must run from a directory containing firebase.json. Use --only or --except to narrow the deploy, and add -m "message" to attach a release note.

Uploads just the Hosting site (the static files from your public directory) and leaves functions, rules, and indexes alone. Faster than a full firebase deploy when you only changed frontend files. Target a single site in multi-site setups with --only hosting:site-name.

Deploys only the Hosting site named my-site, which matters when firebase.json configures multiple sites and you do not want to touch the others. Site names come from firebase hosting:sites:list. Combine with -m to add a release message shown in the console.

Uploads all your Cloud Functions code without touching Hosting, rules, or indexes. Use it when you only changed backend code, since a full deploy rebuilds everything. Narrow further to individual functions with --only functions:functionName.

Deploys only the function named sendWelcomeEmail, which is ideal for iterating on one endpoint without waiting for the rest to build. The function name must match an export in your functions source. Related commands: firebase deploy --only functions deploys all functions, and firebase functions:delete removes one.

Pushes your local firestore.rules file to the active project, replacing the published rules immediately. Rules changes apply to new requests without redeploying functions, but a mistake can lock clients out, so test with the Firestore emulator first. Related: firebase deploy --only firestore:indexes for indexes.

Uploads the index definitions from firestore.indexes.json to the project. Composite indexes are required for queries that combine multiple fields or range filters. Indexes build asynchronously; watch firestore:operations:list or the console to see when they are ready. Related: firebase firestore:indexes lists deployed indexes.

Uploads your storage.rules file, which controls who can read and write objects in Cloud Storage buckets. Rules changes take effect immediately and can break uploads if written incorrectly, so review them carefully. Related commands: firebase deploy --only database deploys Realtime Database rules.

Pushes database.rules.json to the active Realtime Database instance, updating access control for that database. Bad rules can instantly deny all clients, so test locally first. Related: firebase deploy --only firestore:rules covers Cloud Firestore rules instead.

Deploys only the listed targets — here Hosting and Cloud Functions — while skipping rules and indexes. The --only flag accepts a comma-separated list of any deployable target. This is the fastest way to ship frontend plus backend changes together.

Builds your code and validates configuration exactly as a real deploy would, but uploads nothing to the project. It may still enable required APIs on the target project to give accurate validation. Run it before release deploys in CI to catch build errors early.

commands.desc: Deploy with an attached release message
commands.tooltip: Attaches the message v1.2.0 release to the deployment, which is displayed on the Hosting page of the Firebase console and in deployment history. The -m flag is short for --message. It helps teams see what each deploy contains when reviewing release timelines.

Deploys all configured resources except Cloud Functions, which is the inverse of --only. It is handy when a functions deploy would be slow or risky but you still want rules and Hosting shipped. The flag accepts a comma-separated list, for example --except functions,storage.

Runs the deploy against the staging project regardless of the active project set with firebase use. The -P flag (short for --project) works on nearly every firebase command and accepts a project ID or an alias. Use it to promote the same codebase to production with firebase deploy -P prod.

Boots every emulator defined in the emulators block of firebase.json — commonly Firestore, Auth, Functions, and Hosting — so your app runs entirely on localhost. An emulator is a local simulation of the real service, so no production data is touched. Stop them with Ctrl+C; capture state first with firebase emulators:export.

Starts just the Auth and Firestore emulators from your emulator configuration, which is faster and uses less memory than starting everything. The --only flag takes a comma-separated list of emulator names such as auth, firestore, functions, database, storage, or hosting. Useful for frontend-only work that needs a mock backend.

Runs the Cloud Functions emulator, which executes your deployed function code locally on port 5001 by default. Requests are served as if the functions were live, making it great for testing HTTP triggers and callable functions. Pair it with the Firestore emulator (--only functions,firestore) when functions read or write data.

commands.desc: Run a test script against emulators
commands.tooltip: Starts the emulators, runs the quoted command (here npm test), then shuts the emulators down — ideal for CI and one-off test runs. Test code can point at localhost ports without any cleanup steps. Add --only to limit which emulators boot, and --ui to also launch the Emulator UI.

commands.desc: Export emulator data to a directory
commands.tooltip: Saves the current state of running emulators — Firestore documents, Auth users, and more — into ./backup-dir so you can restore it later. Use --only auth,firestore to limit what is exported, and -f to overwrite an existing directory. Restore the data with firebase emulators:start --import ./backup-dir.

commands.desc: Start emulators with previously exported data
commands.tooltip: Boots the emulators and loads the data previously saved by firebase emulators:export from ./backup-dir, giving you a reproducible starting state such as seeded users or documents. The directory contains the firebase-export.json manifest plus per-emulator data folders. Related: --export-on-exit saves state automatically when you quit.

Runs the emulators normally but automatically writes their state to ./backup-dir whenever they shut down cleanly with Ctrl+C. It pairs naturally with --import ./backup-dir to keep a persistent local dataset across sessions. Omit the directory to reuse whatever --import provided.

commands.desc: Debug emulated functions with the Node inspector
commands.tooltip: Starts the Functions emulator in debug mode so you can attach a debugger, such as Chrome DevTools or VS Code, to the Node inspector on port 9229. Set breakpoints in function code and step through requests locally. Related: firebase functions:shell gives a REPL for calling functions directly.

Fetches the Firestore emulator jar so firebase emulators:start can run it locally. The emulator is a Java-based simulation of Cloud Firestore used for offline development and testing. The first emulators:start normally downloads it for you; this command does so explicitly, which helps in restricted network environments.

Downloads the Emulator UI, a local web dashboard (default port 4000) that shows emulator status, lets you inspect Firestore documents, and view Auth users. The UI is bundled separately from the emulators themselves. Launch it with firebase emulators:start --ui or by enabling ui in the emulators config.

Deletes the document at the path users/ada from the default Firestore database and asks for confirmation first. Without the -r flag it refuses to touch subcollections under that document, which protects you from accidental data loss. Add -f to skip the confirmation prompt in scripts.

commands.desc: Recursively delete a document and subcollections
commands.tooltip: Deletes the document users/ada plus every document in all of its subcollections — a powerful and irreversible operation, so the CLI still asks for confirmation unless you add -f. The -r flag (short for --recursive) cannot be combined with --shallow. For wiping an entire collection, prefer firestore:bulkdelete.

commands.desc: Delete only top-level documents in a collection
commands.tooltip: Deletes the documents directly under the users collection but ignores any subcollections, which can orphan nested documents that still reference deleted parents. It is the opposite of -r, and the two flags are mutually exclusive. Use it to clear a collection level while preserving deeper data.

commands.desc: Wipe all data from the Firestore database
commands.tooltip: Deletes every collection and document in the default Firestore database, returning it to an empty state. This is extremely destructive and cannot be undone, and -f skips all confirmation prompts, so double-check the project with firebase use before running it. Consider firestore:export-style backups first.

Prints the composite and single-field indexes defined in your project in the JSON specification format, matching what firestore.indexes.json expects. Add --pretty for a readable table layout. Deploy new index definitions with firebase deploy --only firestore:indexes.

commands.desc: List Firestore indexes in a readable table
commands.tooltip: Displays the project's deployed Firestore indexes as a formatted table with collection, fields, and query scope columns instead of raw JSON. The data is the same as plain firebase firestore:indexes, just easier to scan. Useful when deciding whether a slow query needs a new composite index.

Prints the Google Cloud regions where you can create a Firestore database, such as nam5 (multi-region US) and europe-west3. The list feeds into commands like firestore:databases:create and backup tooling that take a --location argument. Locations also determine data residency for compliance.

Uses Firestore's managed bulk delete service to remove all documents in the posts and comments collection groups — every collection with that name across the database. It is safer and more efficient than firestore:delete for large datasets, and it pauses when no documents match. Confirm the collection IDs carefully since this is irreversible.

commands.desc: List Firestore databases in the project
commands.tooltip: Shows every Cloud Firestore database in the active project, including the default database and any named databases like ecommerce. Projects can host multiple databases, each with independent rules and indexes. Create another with firebase firestore:databases:create.

Creates a new Cloud Firestore database called ecommerce in the default location, separate from the (default) database. Named databases suit multi-tenant or environment-separated designs, and each needs its own rules and indexes configured in firebase.json. Delete one with firestore:databases:delete.

commands.desc: Show details of a Firestore database
commands.tooltip: Prints metadata about the ecommerce database: its type (native or Datastore mode), location, and state. It is a quick way to confirm a named database exists and where it lives before running operations against it. List all databases with firebase firestore:databases:list.

Permanently removes the ecommerce database and all of its data, with a confirmation prompt unless you pass -f. Deleting the (default) database is not supported this way. Consider backups via firestore:backups first, since this operation cannot be undone.

Lists the managed backups available for Firestore databases in the nam5 location, showing each backup's database, creation time, and size. Pass -l to filter by region, or omit it for all locations. Backups are created by schedules you define with firestore:backups:schedules:create.

Shows long-running administrative operations such as index builds and bulk deletes, with their status and progress. It is the CLI window into work Firestore is doing in the background, for example after deploying new composite indexes. Limit the result count with --limit, or scope to a database with --database.

commands.desc: Test functions in a Node REPL
commands.tooltip: Launches the Functions emulator and drops you into an interactive Node shell where you can call your functions directly with test data, including onCall functions and background triggers. It is the fastest way to poke at function behavior without writing an HTTP client. Type the function name plus arguments to invoke it; exit with Ctrl+C or .exit.

Fetches the latest log entries from your deployed Cloud Functions, which is the first stop when a production function fails or returns unexpected results. Logs come from Cloud Logging, so anything your function writes with console.log appears here. Limit the volume with -n 50, or filter to one function with --only.

commands.desc: Read logs for a single function
commands.tooltip: Shows only the log lines produced by the sendWelcomeEmail function, cutting through noise from other functions. The --only flag takes a comma-separated list of function names. Combine with -n to cap how many lines are fetched. Related: firebase functions:list shows all deployed function names.

Limits the fetched logs to the 50 most recent entries instead of the default batch, which keeps output manageable for frequently called functions. The -n flag is short for --lines. Add --only functionName to scope the lines to one function.

Prints every function deployed in the active project along with its region and runtime. It is the authoritative inventory of your backend, handy before a functions:delete or when auditing which endpoints exist. Filters and regions are shown so you can copy exact names into --only deploy filters.

Removes the sendWelcomeEmail function from the project after a confirmation prompt; add -f to skip it. Deleting a function that other code calls will break those callers, so check dependencies first. Pass multiple names or use --region to disambiguate functions with the same name in different regions.

commands.desc: Delete a function in a specific region
commands.tooltip: Deletes the sendWelcomeEmail function only from the europe-west1 region. This matters when the same function name is deployed to several regions — without --region, matching functions in all regions get deleted. Confirm the region list with firebase functions:list.

commands.desc: Create or update a functions secret
commands.tooltip: Creates or rotates the secret STRIPE_API_KEY in Cloud Secret Manager for use by Cloud Functions, prompting for the value or reading it from --data-file. Reference it in code with the functions SDK instead of hardcoding credentials. Secrets are versioned, so rotation creates a new version; access the value with functions:secrets:access.

commands.desc: Set a secret from a file
commands.tooltip: Stores the contents of ./key.txt as the value of the STRIPE_API_KEY secret, which avoids typing sensitive values into your shell history. The CLI prompts to redeploy functions that use the secret unless you pass -f. Related: functions:secrets:get shows metadata and versions for the secret.

commands.desc: Show metadata for a functions secret
commands.tooltip: Prints the metadata for STRIPE_API_KEY, including creation time and every version currently stored, without revealing the secret values themselves. Use it to audit when a secret was rotated and which versions still exist. Access the actual value with functions:secrets:access.

Outputs the latest value of STRIPE_API_KEY (or a specific version with KEY@2 syntax), which is occasionally needed for debugging or manual setup. Anyone with CLI access to the project can read this, so avoid printing secrets in shared logs. Related: functions:secrets:get lists versions first.

Permanently deletes STRIPE_API_KEY (or a specific version with KEY@2 syntax) from Secret Manager after a confirmation prompt. Destroyed secrets cannot be recovered, and functions still referencing the destroyed version will fail, so check functions:secrets:get first. Related: functions:secrets:prune cleans up unused secrets.

commands.desc: Destroy secrets no longer in use
commands.tooltip: Deletes secret versions that no deployed function references, cleaning up credentials left behind by rotations and deletions. It prompts before destroying anything unless you pass -f. Run functions:secrets:get first to review what is about to go. This is the safe way to keep your secret inventory tidy.

Fetches the value stored at the stripe.key path in the old functions config system and prints it as JSON. Google recommends migrating this config to Secret Manager, and functions:config:export automates that move. New projects should use functions:secrets:set instead.

commands.desc: Clone function config from another project
commands.tooltip: Copies the environment config from the my-app-staging project into the active project, which is useful when promoting code from staging to production. Add --only key1,key2 to copy a subset, or --except to skip keys. The legacy config system is being replaced by Secret Manager, so prefer functions:config:export for new setups.

commands.desc: Export function config to Secret Manager
commands.tooltip: Migrates your legacy functions config (functions:config) into Cloud Secret Manager as a single secret, defaulting to the name FUNCTIONS_CONFIG_EXPORT unless you pass --secret NAME. Afterward, functions read the values via the secrets API instead of config. This is the recommended path off the deprecated config system.

commands.desc: Deploy Hosting to a preview channel
commands.tooltip: Deploys your Hosting content to the preview channel named preview1, creating the channel if needed, and prints a unique preview URL like preview1--project-id.web.app. Preview channels are ephemeral environments for sharing work-in-progress with reviewers. The channel expires after 7 days by default; extend or shorten it with --expires.

commands.desc: Deploy a preview channel with a custom lifetime
commands.tooltip: Deploys to the preview1 channel and keeps it alive for 30 days before Firebase deletes it automatically. The --expires flag accepts durations like 12h or 30d with a maximum of 30d; the default is 7d. Useful for long-running feature reviews. Clean up channels early with hosting:channel:delete.

commands.desc: Deploy a preview channel and open it
commands.tooltip: Deploys to the preview1 channel and immediately opens the preview URL in your default browser. It is a handy end-to-end check after shipping a change, saving you from copying the URL out of the deploy output. The channel still expires per --expires, defaulting to 7 days.

commands.desc: List Hosting channels for the project
commands.tooltip: Shows every channel of the default Hosting site, including the permanent live channel and any preview channels, each with its URL and expiration date. Add --site site-name to list channels of a different site. Related: hosting:channel:delete removes a preview channel.

commands.desc: Open a preview channel in the browser
commands.tooltip: Opens the URL of the preview1 channel in your default browser, or prints the URL when a browser is unavailable. It is the quick way to revisit a preview channel you deployed earlier. Add --site site-name if the channel belongs to a non-default site.

Removes the preview1 channel and its deployed version after a confirmation prompt; pass -f to skip it. The live channel cannot be deleted, only preview channels can. Do this to clean up stale preview URLs and stop them from being served.

commands.desc: Create a Hosting channel without deploying
commands.tooltip: Creates the preview1 channel ahead of time without deploying any content to it, so the channel exists with an empty version. This is a stepping stone for workflows that create channels and deploy later, or for reserving a URL. Deploy to it with firebase hosting:channel:deploy preview1.

commands.desc: Promote a preview channel to live
commands.tooltip: Copies the most recently deployed version from the my-site:preview1 channel to the live channel of my-site, effectively promoting a reviewed preview to production without rebuilding. It also works across sites, for example siteA:preview1 siteB:live. Run a quick sanity check on the preview URL before cloning.

Stops serving web traffic for the default Hosting site, showing a temporary maintenance page instead, after a confirmation prompt unless you pass -f. It does not delete the site or its content. Re-enable hosting by deploying again or in the console. Use -s site-name to target a specific site.

commands.desc: List Hosting sites in the project
commands.tooltip: Prints every Firebase Hosting site in the active project with its ID, default domain, and creation date. Projects can hold multiple sites, for example one per environment or brand. Create additional sites with hosting:sites:create.

Creates a Firebase Hosting site named my-site and gives it a default domain, without deploying any content. Sites are independent containers for Hosting versions, useful for multi-site architectures. Deploy to it with firebase deploy --only hosting:my-site after adding it to firebase.json.

commands.desc: Show details of a Hosting site
commands.tooltip: Prints metadata about the my-site Hosting site, such as its ID, default URL, and creation time. It is a quick lookup before managing the site or configuring custom domains. List all sites with firebase hosting:sites:list.

Permanently removes the my-site Hosting site and its deployed versions after a confirmation prompt; -f skips the prompt. Any custom domains pointing at the site stop resolving, so migrate traffic first. Deleting the default site is not allowed.

commands.desc: Export Auth users to a JSON file
commands.tooltip: Downloads every user account from Firebase Authentication into users.json, including UIDs, emails, provider info, and password hashes. The export is the standard way to back up or migrate users. Add --format csv to write comma-separated data instead, and import the file later with firebase auth:import.

commands.desc: Export Auth users to a CSV file
commands.tooltip: Writes all Authentication users to users.csv in comma-separated format, which opens directly in spreadsheets for audits or bulk edits. The file extension selects the format automatically; the --format flag only matters when the filename is ambiguous. Re-import the file with firebase auth:import.

commands.desc: Import users from a JSON file
commands.tooltip: Loads user accounts from users.json into Firebase Authentication, creating or updating them in bulk. If the accounts use password hashes from another system, you must pass the matching hash flags, for example --hash-algo bcrypt. This is the primary tool for migrating users between projects or from a legacy backend.

Imports users.json and tells Firebase their passwords were hashed with bcrypt, so it can verify logins against the imported hashes. Different algorithms need different flags — scrypt needs --rounds and --mem-cost, SHA256 needs --hash-key. Test one account's login after importing to confirm the hash parameters match.

Imports users whose passwords were hashed with scrypt, declaring the exact scrypt parameters used by the source system: 8 rounds and memory cost 14. Firebase must know these values to reproduce the hashes at login time. Getting a parameter wrong makes imported passwords unverifiable, so keep the source settings handy.

commands.desc: Fetch Realtime Database data as JSON
commands.tooltip: Reads the data at the /users path of the active Realtime Database and prints it as JSON. Add --pretty for readable formatting, or -o filename to save to a file. Query options like --order-by and --limit-to-first refine large datasets. Data is served from the live database, so results reflect production state.

commands.desc: Fetch database data with readable formatting
commands.tooltip: Prints the /users path with indented, colorized JSON instead of a compact single line. Handy when inspecting nested records by eye. The data itself is identical to the plain form. Save the formatted output with -o filename if you want to keep it.

commands.desc: Save database data to a file
commands.tooltip: Fetches the data at /users/ada and writes it to ada.json instead of printing to the terminal. The -o flag is short for --output. Useful for backing up a subtree or feeding the file into other tools. Related: database:set reads JSON back in from a file.

commands.desc: Replace data at a database path
commands.tooltip: Replaces everything at /users/ada with the inline JSON provided by -d, after a confirmation prompt unless you pass -f. Any existing children not present in the new data are deleted, so this is destructive to that path. For merging fields instead, use database:update.

commands.desc: Set database data from a JSON file
commands.tooltip: Replaces the data at /users/ada with the contents of users.json, which is convenient for seeding or restoring a subtree. The file argument can also be stdin. Add -f to skip the confirmation prompt, and --disable-triggers to prevent Cloud Functions from firing on the write.

commands.desc: Append data to a database list
commands.tooltip: Adds the JSON object to the /messages list and lets Realtime Database generate a unique push key for it, producing /messages/-NxyzABC. Use push for chat-style append-only lists where you need unique IDs. Related: database:set replaces data at an exact path instead.

commands.desc: Merge fields into an existing record
commands.tooltip: Merges the provided JSON into /users/ada, adding or updating only those keys while leaving all other children untouched. This is the safe counterpart to database:set, which replaces the entire path. The -d flag supplies inline JSON; you can also pass a file path.

commands.desc: Delete data at a database path
commands.tooltip: Removes everything stored at /users/ada, including all nested children, after a confirmation prompt unless you pass -f. There is no undo, so double-check the path — removing / wipes the whole database. Related: database:set can restore data afterward if you have a backup.

commands.desc: Import a JSON file into the database
commands.tooltip: Loads the contents of backup.json into the Realtime Database at the specified path, here the root /, writing records non-atomically in chunks. Unlike database:set it does not first delete existing data at the target, so it is suitable for merging large backups. Tune throughput with --chunk-size and --concurrency.

Streams live operation data from the Realtime Database and produces a usage report showing read, write, and latency statistics per path. Run it while traffic flows to find hot spots and slow queries. Set a collection window with -d 30 for 30 seconds, or analyze a saved log with -i filename.

Collects Realtime Database usage statistics for 30 seconds, then prints a report of read/write volume and latency grouped by path. The -d flag sets the duration in seconds. Useful for capturing a bounded sample during a load test. Save the report with -o filename.

Shows every Realtime Database instance in the project with its name and location. A project can hold multiple named instances beyond the default, each with independent data and rules. Filter by region with -l europe-west1. Create new instances with database:instances:create.

Creates a new Realtime Database instance named my-app-eu in the europe-west1 region, useful for geographic data residency or separating workloads. Without -l it defaults to us-central1. The instance gets its own rules and data, managed via the --instance flag on other database commands.

Prints the current value of the defaultWriteSizeLimit setting, which caps how large a single write can be before it is rejected. It is the CLI way to inspect database-level settings. Change the value with database:settings:set.

Sets the defaultWriteSizeLimit setting to unlimited, removing the size cap on individual writes to the database. Other accepted values are small, medium, and large. Raising the limit lets bigger payloads through but can increase cost and latency, so prefer the smallest value your app needs.

commands.desc: List apps registered in the project
commands.tooltip: Shows every app registered in the active Firebase project — web, Android, and iOS — with its platform, display name, and app ID. App IDs look like 1:123456789:android:abc123 and are required by many other commands. Filter the list by passing a platform such as ANDROID.

commands.desc: List only Android apps in the project
commands.tooltip: Filters the project's apps down to the Android platform, showing each app's package name and app ID. The platform argument is case-insensitive and also accepts IOS or WEB. The app ID output feeds directly into apps:sdkconfig and appdistribution:distribute.

commands.desc: Print the Android config file contents
commands.tooltip: Prints the google-services.json contents for the Android app with ID 1:123456789:android:abc123, which apps embed to connect to Firebase. Add -o google-services.json to write it straight to a file. This is how you fetch app config without opening the console. WEB apps get a config snippet instead.

commands.desc: Save the web app config to a file
commands.tooltip: Writes the Firebase web config for app 1:123456789:web:def456 to firebase-config.js instead of printing it. The config contains the apiKey, projectId, and other values you pass to initializeApp. Download it after creating a new web app to wire up the frontend.

Registers an Android app named MyApp with the package name com.example.myapp in the active project and prints its new app ID. The --package-name flag is required for Android apps; iOS uses --bundle-id instead. After registering, fetch config with apps:sdkconfig.

Creates a web app named MyWebApp in the active project and prints its app ID plus the config snippet to paste into your JavaScript. Web apps need no extra identifier, unlike Android and iOS apps. Pull the config again anytime with apps:sdkconfig WEB.

commands.desc: Download config for an existing app
commands.tooltip: Downloads the google-services.json for the Android app 1:123456789:android:abc123 and saves it into the current directory, or wherever -o points. It is a quick way to bootstrap a new checkout without hunting through the console. Related: apps:sdkconfig prints the same config to stdout.

commands.desc: Upload a build to App Distribution
commands.tooltip: Uploads app-release.apk to Firebase App Distribution for the app 1:123456789:android:abc123, making it available to testers you select. Add --release-notes "message" to describe the build, and --testers or --groups to send invites immediately. App Distribution is Google's channel for handing pre-release builds to testers.

commands.cmd: firebase appdistribution:distribute app-release.apk --app 1:123456789:android:abc123 --release-notes "Bug fixes and polish"
commands.desc: Upload a release with release notes
commands.tooltip: Uploads app-release.apk and attaches the note Bug fixes and polish, which testers see on their install page and in the invite email. Release notes default to empty, so set them for any build that goes to a team. Related: --release-notes-file reads the note from a file.

commands.desc: Distribute a build to specific testers
commands.tooltip: Uploads app-release.apk and immediately invites the listed email addresses to test it, so testers get an install link without you using the console. Emails are comma-separated; use --testers-file with a text file for long lists. Group-based distribution uses --groups instead.

commands.desc: Add a tester to the project
commands.tooltip: Registers alice@example.com as a tester in App Distribution so she can be invited to future releases. Add --group-alias qa to also place her in the qa group, or --file testers.txt to bulk-add from a list. Manage the roster with appdistribution:testers:list and testers:remove.

Shows every tester registered in the project, optionally filtered to one group by passing the group alias. Testers are the people who receive your pre-release builds. Related: appdistribution:testers:add invites new ones and appdistribution:testers:remove revokes access.

commands.desc: Remove a tester from the project
commands.tooltip: Revokes alice@example.com's access to future App Distribution releases; existing installed builds keep working but she no longer receives new ones. Pass --group-alias to remove her from a group instead of the whole project. Check who is registered with appdistribution:testers:list first.

Creates a tester group named QA Team with the alias qa, which you can then pass to --groups on appdistribution:distribute to send builds to the whole team at once. The alias must be unique in the project. Add members with appdistribution:testers:add --group-alias qa.

Uploads native debug symbols from ./build/symbols so Crashlytics can symbolicate (turn memory addresses into readable function names) for crashes in native code like C++ or Flutter engine code. The --app flag names the target app and --generator picks the symbol format. Run it as part of your release build.

Uploads the R8/ProGuard mapping.txt so Crashlytics can deobfuscate stack traces from release Android builds, where class and method names are stripped. Upload the mapping that shipped with each release version, or crashes stay unreadable. The companion crashlytics:mappingfile:generateid creates the mapping file ID resource.

Adds the storage-resize-images extension to the project: it configures the extension's parameters interactively, registers it in firebase.json, and can deploy it immediately. Extensions are packaged backend features you install without writing code. Manage them with ext:list, ext:update, and ext:uninstall.

Updates the storage-resize-images extension instance to the latest version, or to a specific version if you pass one after the instance ID. Extensions ship fixes and new features as new versions. Check the current version with ext:list before updating.

Shows every extension installed in the active project, with its instance ID, extension reference, and version. Instance IDs are what ext:update and ext:uninstall expect as arguments. Browse the marketplace at firebase.google.com/products/extensions before installing new ones.

Removes the storage-resize-images extension instance from the project, including the resources it created, after a confirmation prompt unless you pass -f. Uninstalling can delete data the extension produced, like resized images, so back up anything you need first.

Turns on the webframeworks experiment for this machine, which unlocks beta CLI behavior such as deploying Next.js and Angular apps to Hosting. Experiments are unstable features that can change without notice. List what is available with experiments:list and switch it off with experiments:disable.

Turns off the webframeworks experiment on this machine, restoring default CLI behavior. Disable an experiment when a beta feature causes deploy or build problems. See the current state of all experiments with experiments:list.

commands.desc: List CLI experiments and their state
commands.tooltip: Prints every available CLI experiment with a short description and whether it is currently enabled on this machine. Experiments gate beta features that are not stable enough for defaults. Toggle them with experiments:enable and experiments:disable.

Downloads the active Remote Config template as JSON, showing all parameters, conditions, and the version number. Remote Config lets you change app behavior without shipping a new build. Fetch a specific historical version with -v VERSION and save to a file with -o.

Shows the five most recent published versions of the Remote Config template with timestamps and update sources. Pass --limit 0 to list every version ever published. Version numbers from this list feed remoteconfig:rollback -v.

commands.desc: Roll back Remote Config to a version
commands.tooltip: Reverts the published Remote Config template to version 42, after a confirmation prompt unless you pass -f. Rollbacks are themselves new versions, so they appear in versions:list. Use this when a bad parameter change broke clients. Omit -v to roll back one version.

Shows every Firebase App Hosting backend in the project, which are the server-rendered deployment targets for frameworks like Next.js. Each backend ties a Git repository and build to a live URL. Create one with apphosting:backends:create after firebase init apphosting.
